questions.question: What does it mean for two metrics $d_p$ and $d_q$ on $\boldsymbol X$ to be topologically equivalent?
options: They give exactly the same distance between every pair of points.
They produce the same collection of open subsets of $\boldsymbol X$.
They are both discrete metrics.
They make every subset of $\boldsymbol X$ finite.
questions.explanation: Two metrics are topologically equivalent when they produce the same collection of open subsets of $\boldsymbol{X}$.

questions.question: Which pair of metrics is topologically equivalent but not strongly equivalent?
options: The discrete metric is topologically equivalent to every $p$-metric.
Strongly equivalent metrics are never topologically equivalent.
Topologically equivalent metrics must have equal distance values.
$d_{\tan}(x,y)=|\tan x-\tan y|$ is topologically equivalent to $|\cdot|$, not strongly.
questions.explanation: $d_{\tan}(x,y)=|\tan x-\tan y|$ is topologically equivalent to the absolute-value metric on $\mathbb{R}$ (they determine the same open sets) but not strongly equivalent, since no global constants $a,b$ can bound $d_{\tan}$ relative to $|\cdot|$ near the asymptotes of $\tan$.
questions.source_support: Topologically Equivalent Metrics page: definition, interpretation, strong equivalence implication, and examples.

questions.question: If a sequence convergence statement is based only on open sets and two metrics are topologically equivalent, which expectation is natural?
options: It should be unchanged under replacing one metric by the other.
The statement must reverse direction.
The sequence must become finite.
The two metrics must be strongly equivalent first.
questions.explanation: A convergence statement based only on open sets is unchanged when one topologically equivalent metric is replaced by the other, since the two metrics share the same open sets.
questions.source_support: Topologically equivalent metrics agree on open sets and hence on topological notions.
option_explanations: The statement is unchanged, not reversed in direction; replacing a metric with a topologically equivalent one preserves all topological notions.
The sequence need not become finite; topological equivalence preserves convergence behaviour without restricting sequences to be finite.
Topological equivalence alone suffices to preserve open-set-based statements; strong equivalence is a stronger condition that is not required.
